725.t: Listening to the original record and Bright Star
725.s: Comparing the scratchy copy to the original, Piron's solos, and Pete's Bright Star used to open their vaudeville program.
725.q: Yeah. He... Yeah, that's the original, I reckon. We had another number we made. We had used it for the opening of our program in Vaudeville. Oh, that's it. Bright Star was the name. You ever heard that thing? That was a beautiful thing. Yeah. It was beautiful. Pete wrote that. Bright Star. That was…

786.t: Forgetting old record lyrics and never reading music
786.s: Shade cannot recall the words of one of his records, remembers titles but not tunes, and says he has never read music.
786.q: I never forgot the title, almost, songs and everything. It's how the tune I played them in and everything. Playing by air, you can't keep up with your tune.

203.s: They play a recording and try to identify the lead trumpeter.
203.q: Of course they’re copying note for note, whoever it is. That’s why it sounds funny.

787.s: Rowe praises hearing new countermelodies on a second listen; Broadbent notes the second movement uses the same theme upside down.
787.q: But then again the second movement is kind of a movement d’amore. But it’s the same theme only cleverly composed upside-down which people will eventually get.

206.t: Hoagy Carmichael track and a family link
206.s: He chose a Carmichael tune and explains his family link and his admiration.
206.q: I’ll tell you later why I picked this out of this particular set. There’s a reason, not because of my playing, I mean because of a social explanation.

788.s: Rowe thanks Harris for recording Hutcherson's 'Now'; Harris says it is a platform for many voices and unites the ensemble.
788.q: Yeah. What a fantastic piece of music, and it functions in the exact way that you hope that any great piece of music will function in that it becomes this phenomenal platform for the expression of a myriad of voices. It’s a so beautiful melody that it’s repeated with an absolutely perfect harmony…

562.t: Playing a track of her CD
562.s: Rowe plays an excerpt of one of her recordings and notes the improvised passage and her low register.

789.s: Rowe plays an excerpt of Levy's concerto and praises its tunes and the harmonica's unison tone colors.

733.s: Rowe plays 'As Time Goes By' from the CD and points out a modulation in the last A section that Person does not recall.
733.q: A Houston Person sound, oh. Let me hear this so I can learn it.

790.s: Player praises the show's authenticity, and Rowe tells of a realistic amp detail.
790.q: I think they’ve done an excellent job in trying to capture it. It’s the closest thing — and it’s funny because I wasn’t born in New Orleans, it’s interesting when I talk to a lot of my colleagues who, maybe who are New Orleanians, they’re very, very protective in ways, of their culture. So when you…

396.t: Playing Bach at Hamilton and her poor retention of music
396.s: Rowe recalls her being unable to speak after a Bach piece at Hamilton; she worries she remembers little of the music she hears.
396.q: I hope so. I criticize myself because I have a terrible — you know most of my friends who are musicians, everyone in Italy but also most of my friends here, you know remember every album they’ve listened to, the name, the cuts, who played on them, they’ve got it all catalogued, you know, what they…

364.s: Playback of a track with Harry Allen and Dan Barrett, noting written and open parts.
364.q: The solos aren’t. That’s Harry Allen and Dan Barrett. Slips through three chords.

80.t: Una Mae Carlisle, 'Walking by the River', and Stuff's carnival and banjo past
80.s: Stuff claimed to have written 'Walking by the River' for Una Mae Carlisle; he began as a banjoist and carnival player, and said Autrey looked like his father.
80.ch: Hopkins, the South and Stuff Smith
80.q: And maybe he did, and maybe he didn't. And he told me, about -- hmmmmm, we played -- I played, -- I don't play, but all the bands I've played played it, he said he wrote that, which he could have, as far as that goes. I mean you know, he was capable of writing anything, because Stuff was a heck of…

418.t: Never playing piano again and remembering song lyrics
418.s: He never played piano professionally again, could only accompany his own singing, and forgets lyrics over time.
418.ch: Technique and life on the road (repeated passages)
418.q: No, no, I didn't. No. After that I wouldn't dare. I wouldn't dare. I would sound like a beginner. But if I was singing, I could just halfway accompany myself, you know.
